   - Put on rubber gloves if you have them.

   - Pause 30–60 seconds and repeat several rounds.

Here’s how to handle this toilet as safely as possible:

1. Lower the bowl water (if it’s still very high)  
   - Put on rubber gloves.  
   - Use a small container (plastic cup or similar) to scoop water from the bowl into a bucket until the level is a few inches below the rim.  
   - Set that bucket aside for now—don’t pour it into another drain yet.

2. Plunge the right way  
   - Ideally use a toilet plunger (with a narrow flange/funnel at the bottom). A flat sink plunger is much less effective.  
   - Make sure the rubber part is fully under water; add a bit from your bucket if needed so the cup is covered.  
   - Place the plunger over the hole to form a tight seal.  
   - First press down gently to force out air, then plunge firmly in and out (without breaking the seal) for about 15–20 seconds.  
   - Lift the plunger and see whether the water level drops or starts to swirl down.  
   - Repeat this in several rounds—5–10 rounds is normal for a stubborn clog.

3. Test carefully  
   - Turn the shutoff valve behind the toilet on just long enough to let the tank refill once, then turn it back off so it can’t keep refilling.  
   - Do ONE test flush while watching the bowl closely:  
     - If the water drains down quickly and refills to a normal level, the clog is likely cleared.  
     - If it starts rising toward the rim again, don’t wait for it to overflow—close the shutoff fully and do not flush again. At that point, call a plumber.

4. Clean and disinfect  
   - Soak up all standing water on the floor with old towels or a mop.  
   - Clean the floor and any splashed surfaces first with hot, soapy water, then disinfect (bleach solution or bathroom disinfectant).  
   - Wash used towels on a hot cycle and dry completely.

Call a local plumber as an emergency if:
- Plunging (multiple solid rounds) doesn’t bring the water level down or let the toilet drain, or  
- The toilet repeatedly threatens to overflow on test flushes, or  
- Any other drains start gurgling or backing up later.

<action type="say">
You’re set up well: that flange plunger is exactly what you want, and having the water just below the rim is good.

I can’t dispatch or book a plumber through this system—only guide you—so if this doesn’t clear it, you’ll need to call a local emergency plumber directly.

Use your plunger like this:

1. Seat the plunger
- Pull the little funnel (flange) all the way out so it points straight down.
- Place the flange straight into the hole at the bottom of the bowl so it fits snugly.
- Tilt the plunger slightly as you press down the first time to let trapped air escape—you want water inside the cup, not air.

2. Plunge with a tight seal
- Once seated, hold the handle mostly vertical to keep the seal.
- Start with a few slow, gentle pushes to firm up the seal.
- Then do firm in‑and‑out strokes for about 15–20 seconds without breaking the seal. Focus on moving water through the clog, not just slamming the plunger.
- After the first round, lift the plunger:
  - If you hear a “glug” and the water level drops, that’s a good sign—do another couple of rounds to fully clear it.
  - If the level barely changes, reseat and repeat another 15–20 second round.

Do several rounds like this—5–10 solid rounds is normal for a stubborn clog.

3. Safe test flush
- When the bowl water level clearly drops toward normal:
  - Turn the shutoff valve behind the toilet back on just long enough for the tank to refill, then turn it off again so it can’t keep refilling.
  - Do ONE test flush while watching closely:
    - If the water swirls down quickly and refills to a normal level, you’ve likely cleared it—then you can turn the shutoff fully back on.
    - If the water starts rising instead of draining, quickly close the shutoff, don’t flush again, and call a plumber.

If you try a good 5–10 plunging rounds and the bowl still won’t drain or keeps threatening to overflow on test flushes, stop and contact a local emergency plumber—it likely needs professional equipment.

If you tell me what happens after 2–3 good plunging rounds (does the water level drop at all, any “glug” sounds?), I can help you interpret what’s going on. </action>
